title: The Long Count
sketch: F: deep-time counting song. Each verse tallies one singer by order of magnitude (the first, the tenth, the hundredth, the billionth) and the two who heard it: one branch dies, one carries it on, usually wrongly. Steady 4/4 in phrygian. The refrain is the fossil: a tally that climbs the tonic triad until 'one' lands on the octave, and a hum that walks back down.
refrain: One, and one, and one, and one,
ev-ery mouth that sang is gone;
sing it once and you're the sum:
hum, and hum, and hum, and hum.

lines: The [ordinal, two syllables: 'first one', 'tenth one', 'hun-dredth', 'mil-lionth'] sang it [where, four syllables, weak weak STRONG weak: 'in a kitch-en', 'down from or-bit'],
to [a hearer, two syllables] and [the other hearer, one syllable];
[what became of the first hearer: the branch that died]
[what the second hearer did with it: the branch that carried on, rhyming with line 2]
verse_template.note: The ordinals climb by orders of magnitude and never come back down. Hearers can be anyone or anything: people, weather, animals, machines, the moon, the dust. The first hearer always loses it (dies, forgets, files it as noise); the second keeps it, usually wrongly (out of key, without the words, a single tone). Late verses go past the words altogether: the tune is older than the language, and only the hum part is safe. Deadpan; the cosmic scale is the joke.

hooks.why: the tally climbs the tonic triad, one-and one-and one-and, and 'one' lands on the octave, which is one again
the hum walks down onto the phrygian cadence, flat two to one, the last word of the fossil
'you're the sum' lifts to the flat ninth, the highest and strangest note in the song

seed_verses: The first one sang it in a kitch-en
to a ba-by and the rain;
the rain for-got it in the gut-ter;
the ba-by sang it back a-gain.
The tenth one sang it on a fer-ry
to a stran-ger and the sea;
the stran-ger died in nine-teen-some-thing;
the sea still hums it, out of key.
The hun-dredth sang it in a lan-guage
to a daugh-ter and the birds;
the daugh-ter was the last who spoke it;
the birds went on with-out the words.
The thou-sandth sang it down from or-bit
to a night shift and the moon;
the night shift wrote it down as stat-ic;
the moon kept time and kept the tune.
The mil-lionth sang it on some plan-et
to the si-lence and the dust;
the si-lence was-n't in-ter-est-ed;
the dust hummed on, as all dust must.
The bil-lionth sang it in a lan-guage
that no one has heard of yet;
the words were new, the tune was an-cient,
the hum part noth-ing can for-get.
